summary: Describes LDAP schema for representing X.509 certificates, X.521 security information and related elements in directories. These replace the definitions in RFC 2252 and RFC 2256. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Instructions for storing digital ID cards in an address book so others can look them up.

subtitle: How LDAP directories store and search X.509 certificates, revocation lists and related security data.

tldr.problem: Directories reached through LDAP needed a standard way to hold X.509 certificates, certificate revocation lists and related security information, and the older definitions were out of date.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines LDAP syntaxes, matching rules, attribute types and object classes for a subset of X.509 and X.521, with certificates carried as DER values using the binary transfer option.
tldr.outcome: It replaces the X.509 schema in RFC 2252 and RFC 2256 and obsoletes RFC 2587. It adds the pkiUser, pkiCA and deltaCRL classes and deprecates older classes in favor of pkiUser and pkiCA.

today: RFC 4523 is a Proposed Standard and is not marked as obsoleted or updated. It replaces the X.509 schema parts of RFC 2252 and RFC 2256 and obsoletes RFC 2587.

sections.title: What This Schema Covers
sections.content:
RFC 4523 gives LDAP schema definitions for a subset of the elements in X.509 and X.521. It covers attribute types for certificates, cross certificate pairs and certificate revocation lists, matching rules for those attributes, related object classes, and LDAP syntaxes for the assertion and attribute values.

The meaning of each element is the one given in X.509 and X.521, so the RFC says that knowledge of those standards is needed to use the schema. Definitions are written in the LDAP description formats of RFC 4512.

Together with RFC 4510, it obsoletes RFC 2252 and RFC 2256 in their entirety, and it obsoletes RFC 2587. Changes since the older RFCs include new classes pkiUser, pkiCA and deltaCRL, equality matching rules added to attribute types, new certificate matching rules, and LDAP syntaxes for their assertions.
sections.eli5: The directory is a giant phone book. This document explains how to file digital ID cards in it, and it replaces older, out-of-date filing instructions.

sections.title: Syntaxes for Certificates and Assertions
sections.content:
Four syntaxes carry the data itself: Certificate, CertificateList, CertificatePair and SupportedAlgorithm. None has an LDAP-specific encoding, because the underlying X.509 definitions changed over time. Values SHOULD be encoded with the Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER) and MUST only be transferred using the ;binary transfer option of RFC 4522, for example userCertificate;binary.

Because these values contain digitally signed data, the value and its form MUST be preserved exactly as presented.

Seven more syntaxes describe assertion values used when searching: the exact and general assertions for certificates, certificate pairs and certificate lists, plus AlgorithmIdentifier. These MUST be encoded with the Generic String Encoding Rules (GSER) of RFC 3641, and Appendix A gives equivalent ABNF grammars.
sections.eli5: A signed ID card must be stored exactly as it was handed over, with no touching up. Search requests have their own written format, so the directory knows what to compare.

sections.title: Matching Rules
sections.content:
Seven matching rules let a client compare a presented assertion with a stored value, in accordance with their X.500 counterparts. They come in pairs: an exact match and a more flexible match for certificates (certificateExactMatch, certificateMatch), certificate pairs (certificatePairExactMatch, certificatePairMatch) and certificate lists (certificateListExactMatch, certificateListMatch).

The seventh, algorithmIdentifierMatch, compares an algorithm identifier with a supported algorithm value. Each rule names the X.509 clause it follows and the assertion syntax it uses.
sections.eli5: Matching rules are the ways to check if two ID cards are the same card, either by an exact look or by a looser comparison of certain details.

sections.title: Attribute Types
sections.content:
Seven attribute types hold the data.

  • userCertificate: certificates issued to the user by one or more certificate authorities.
  • cACertificate: certificates issued to the certificate authority (CA).
  • crossCertificatePair: an X.509 certificate pair.
  • certificateRevocationList, authorityRevocationList and deltaRevocationList: certificate lists.
  • supportedAlgorithms: supported algorithms.

Each has an equality matching rule and an object identifier. For example userCertificate is 2.5.4.36 and uses certificateExactMatch. Values are requested and transferred with the ;binary option, such as cACertificate;binary.
sections.eli5: These are the labeled drawers in the cabinet: one for people's ID cards, one for the issuer's cards, and several for lists of cards that have been cancelled.

sections.title: Object Classes
sections.content:
Eight object classes say which attributes an entry may hold. Most are auxiliary, meaning they augment an existing entry.

  • pkiUser augments entries for objects that may be subject to certificates and may hold userCertificate.
  • pkiCA augments entries for certificate authorities and may hold CA certificates, revocation lists and cross certificate pairs.
  • cRLDistributionPoint is the one structural class. It requires cn and may hold the three revocation lists.
  • deltaCRL augments entries to hold delta revocation lists.
  • userSecurityInformation augments entries with supportedAlgorithms.

Three older classes remain but are deprecated: strongAuthenticationUser in favor of pkiUser, and certificationAuthority and certificationAuthority-V2 in favor of pkiCA.
sections.eli5: Object classes are the forms that say which drawers an entry is allowed to use. Three old forms are still around but should not be used for new work.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
General certificate considerations from RFC 3280 and general LDAP security considerations from RFC 4510 apply. Certificate information is commonly signed, but those signatures only protect the integrity of the signed information.

Without data integrity protection in LDAP or a lower layer such as IPsec, a server cannot be sure a request arrived unaltered, and a client cannot be sure the results were unaltered. The RFC therefore generally recommends using the authentication and data integrity services in LDAP.
sections.eli5: A signature protects the ID card, but not the trip to the directory. Use a safe, checked connection when asking for one.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The IANA registered an LDAP object identifier for the schema elements introduced here and updated the LDAP Descriptor registry. The table of descriptors lists each matching rule, attribute type and object class with its object identifier, and marks the attribute types and object classes as updating earlier registrations.
sections.eli5: The official list of names and numbers was updated so every item in this schema has its own registered entry.
